questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors
questions.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is given by $⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+9{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ Find $⟨x,y⟩$, if

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the inner product according to the definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & =2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+9{x}_{3}{y}_{3} \\  & =2\cdot 1\cdot 5+(-2)\cdot 3+9\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =10-6+9 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors in a Vector Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$ Find $⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}]-[\frac{1}{3}(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors in a Vector Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ].$ Find $⟨t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =0+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,2],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,2].$ Find $⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t{e}^{t}){|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2{e}^{2}-0{e}^{0})-{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2}-({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\frac{\pi }{2},0],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\frac{\pi }{2},0].$ Find $⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{(1)^{3}}{3}]-[-\frac{(0)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,0],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,0].$ Find $⟨t,\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨t,\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}t\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1-{t}^{2},$ $\text{d}u=-2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}t\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3/2}]-[-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3/2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors in a Vector Space of Continuous Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,2\pi\right],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,2\pi\right].$ Find $\langle \sin t, \cos t \rangle$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
\langle \sin t, \cos t \rangle  =  \int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin{t} \cos{t} \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\sin2t =2\sin t\cos t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
